Tell the time the everyday way (Viertel nach, halb, Viertel vor) and the official way (14:30 Uhr).
Understand the “halb” trap: halb acht = 7:30, not 8:30!
Use the days of the week with “am”: am Montag.
Count up to 100, with the units before the tens (einundzwanzig).
Ask for prices and say them.
Ask questions with and without a question word.
It's Saturday morning. Mara goes down to Lena's bakery to buy breakfast. Mr Brandt is already there, with Fritz.
Good morning, Mara! You're early! It's only quarter past seven.
Yes, I always wake up early. How much are the bread rolls?
A bread roll costs forty-five cents. The pretzels cost ninety cents.
Then I'll take four bread rolls and a pretzel. And what's this?
It's plum cake. A piece costs two euros eighty.
Take the cake, Ms Ionescu! Lena's plum cake is the best in Berlin.
OK, and a piece of cake. How much is that?
Here you go. Tell me, Lena, when is the bakery open?
Monday to Friday from half past six until six p.m. On Saturdays until two p.m. On Sunday it's closed.
And on Sunday we'll have breakfast together at my place, Ms Ionescu. At ten o'clock. Fritz insists!
The tens end in “-zig”, read “-tsikh” (with the soft “ch”): zwanzig = “TSVAN-tsikh”, vierzig = “FEER-tsikh”.
“Euro” is read “OY-ro”, not “YOO-ro” as in English!
German says numbers “back to front”: first the unit, then “und”, then the tens, all in one word. 45 = fünfundvierzig = “five-and-forty”.
Watch out for sechzig (60, without the “s”) and siebzig (70, without “en”). And 1 in compounds is “ein”: einundzwanzig, not “einsundzwanzig”.
When you hear a number, wait for the end! “Sieben…” can turn into “siebenundachtzig” (87).
For prices, you say the number of euros, the word “Euro”, then the number of cents, without the word “Cent”:
How much are the bread rolls? (plural: kosten)
In Germany people still pay a lot in cash, especially in small bakeries. It's worth always having some coins on you.
Question: “Wie spät ist es?” or “Wie viel Uhr ist es?” Answer: “Es ist…”.
The trap: “halb neun” = half TOWARDS nine = 8:30. Careful: in British English “half nine” means 9:30, so you could turn up an hour late!
For “at … o'clock” you use “um”: “um zehn Uhr” = at ten o'clock. “Von … bis …” = from … until …
All days are masculine (der Montag) and are used with “am” (= an dem): am Montag = on Monday. “Montags” (with -s) = every Monday, on Mondays.
Times of day: am Morgen (in the morning), am Vormittag (late morning, before noon), am Mittag (at midday), am Nachmittag (in the afternoon), am Abend (in the evening), but: in der Nacht (at night).
Ist die Bäckerei am Sonntag geöffnet?
New W-words: wann? (when?), wie viel? (how much?), wie viele? (how many?), um wie viel Uhr? (at what time?).
To a negative question you answer “doch” if the answer is positive: “Bist du nicht müde?” — “Doch!” (Yes, I am!).
How do you say 9:15 in everyday speech?
On Saturdays I work until two p.m.
Um wie viel Uhr frühstücken sie am Sonntag?
Fritz doesn't have a watch, but Fritz always knows what time it is.
At half past six, Lena opens the bakery. Fritz smells the bread rolls and barks: “Woof!” That means: breakfast!
At eight, Mr Brandt goes to the park with Fritz. Every day, on Sundays too, and in the rain.
At twelve it's lunch. Fritz sits in the kitchen and waits.
In the afternoon, Fritz sleeps on the sofa. Mr Brandt says: “It's not your sofa!” Fritz doesn't hear a thing.
And at quarter past three? At quarter past three, Mara comes home from work.
Fritz sits in front of the door. He waits. He knows: Mara often has something in her bag.
Today is Tuesday. On Tuesdays, Mara works until seven in the evening. But Fritz doesn't know that.
Fritz waits at three. He waits at four. He waits at five. At six he's very sad.
At twenty past seven the door opens. Mara! Fritz jumps, barks and dances.
Mara laughs: “Fritz, you don't have a watch, but you have a big heart.” And then she gives him a piece of sausage.
Bis wann arbeitet Mara am Dienstag?
